title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents

StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and

paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for
improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic
benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the
reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We
introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent
runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce
backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under
uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and
fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent
acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use,
under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function
of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass
thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward
is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode
replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven
frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated
year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model
matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best,
DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic’s
97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore
every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated
year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic
performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B
trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the
held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example
training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and
verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are
withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.10942v1 [cs.AI] 07 Oct 2026 StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents Daksh Raghuvanshi Ved Vedere Yifan Wang † \dagger Abstract Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic’s 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards now drives much of the progress in reasoning and agentic large language models (LLMs) ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Lambert et al., 2025 ) . The tasks and evaluators that supply those rewards therefore increasingly shape what models learn. Meanwhile, AI agents are moving from answering questions to doing real work: their task horizon has doubled roughly every seven months ( Kwa et al., 2025 ) , and evaluations are beginning to cover deliverables drawn from real occupations ( Patwardhan et al., 2025 ) . Yet most agent benchmarks still test bounded tasks in controlled environments that are reset between runs ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) . As a result, they rarely measure what ongoing work requires: sustained reliability, adaptation to change, and the ability to operate with limited human supervision. Reliable operations are fundamental to organizational success. Whether AI agents can excel at them is therefore a critical test of their real-world capabilities. However, operational work breaks the conventional evaluation recipe in three ways. First, the world moves on its own: demand arrives whether or not the agent is ready, deadlines approach, and information goes stale. The environment’s clock must therefore advance independently of both agent actions and inference speed. Second, operational success is cumulative, not binary, and must be measured on a scale calibrated against an external baseline. Third, open-ended rewards invite open-ended gaming: mismatches between the simulator’s rules and its intended behavior create loopholes that reward optimization can teach agents to exploit. Together, these challenges create a need for evaluations of sustained operations under asynchronous demand, with empirically calibrated success criteria and rewards explicitly stress-tested for exploits. We therefore introduce StoreBench , a long-horizon benchmark in which an agent operates a mid-sized online apparel store for 30 to 365 simulated days (Figure 1 ). The environment combines 18 months of operating history, a 40-vendor supplier market, 29 merchant tools, hidden demand, and scripted shocks to suppliers, costs, and competitors within a production-grade commerce backend. Simulated time depends only on agent operations, not inference latency. Scripted policies calibrate each task-seed score and pass threshold, while an exploiter policy tests resistance to known reward hacking. Our contributions are threefold. • A realistic agent environment for long-horizon operational work. The framework of StoreBench is general: its modular tools, event models, and backend can be adapted to other real-world operational settings. • Calibrated, exploit-resistant evaluation. Regression tests cover every known exploit, any run can be replayed for audit, and dense rewards make StoreBench suitable for RL. • An unsaturated benchmark with actionable failure modes. We evaluate frontier models on tasks calibrated to a difficulty that still separates them: none matches the smart-triage operator on average. Replayable traces turn that headroom into concrete targets for improving models and harnesses. A harness-agnostic commerce agent reaches the world only through 29 MCP tools; each call spends one operation, and the world advances in 12-hour windows. The Ostrelle store and its supplier market run on live Medusa v2 software, while demand, order flow, scripted events, and rivals sit in a hidden market the agent observes only through its own sales. Episodes of 30 to 365 days receive weighted scores and are compared to scripted anchor policies. Human experts operate the same MCP surface through a thin GUI, under the same budgets and grading. Icons: Microsoft Fluent Emoji (MIT License). 2 Related work Agent benchmarks. Most agent benchmarks evaluate predefined goals in environments that change only when the agent acts, including software repair ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , web and desktop tasks ( Deng et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) , tool-use dialogues ( Yao et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) , simulated workplace tasks ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , and general-assistant suites ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Mialon et al., 2024 ) . DAYJOB extends this paradigm to multi-hour professional assignments graded with expert rubrics ( Surge AI, 2026 ) , but the unit of evaluation remains a fixed assignment. These benchmarks primarily measure whether an agent completes the task and reaches an end state, not the quality it sustains as demands change. Dynamic operational environments. Gaia2 introduces scripted events that occur independently of the agent, but still evaluates discrete assistant tasks against an oracle action graph ( Froger et al., 2026 ) . Its Time scenarios are capped at five minutes, and generation latency affects the clock: removing it raises GPT-5’s score from 0% to 34.4%. Vending-Bench ( Backlund & Petersson, 2025 ) and MerchantBench ( Shi et al., 2026 ) evaluate long-running businesses using terminal financial outcomes, without task-specific calibrated scales or pass thresholds. Together these gaps point to a need for long-horizon evaluation that meters time through operations rather than generation latency, runs on a production-grade commerce backend, and calibrates each task-seed pair against measured policy baselines. Reward hacking. Reward hacking is a longstanding concern in RL safety ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Krakovna et al., 2020 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ; Pan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) , and LLM agents have been observed modifying rewards and tests, tampering with evaluators, and exploiting feedback loops ( Denison et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Baker et al., 2025 ; Von Arx et al., 2025 ) . Recent benchmarks measure how often such behavior occurs ( Zhong et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Thaman, 2026 ) . However, an open-ended reward needs hardening by design, with each closed exploit fixed by a regression test and calibration failing whenever an exploiter policy beats an honest baseline. 3 The StoreBench environment StoreBench places the agent in charge of Ostrelle , a fictional mid-size online apparel store, for a contiguous shift of 30 to 365 simulated days. The store is not a mock: it runs on Medusa v2, a production-grade open-source commerce platform ( Medusa, 2024 ) , with the agent acting through the same administrative API surface a human operator would use. One container image holds the backend, simulation engine, and tool server; the agent’s network can reach the tool surface and nothing else. 3.1 A world with history The store opens with 18 months of coherent operating history baked into the backend’s own database: 3,320 orders with seasonal and diurnal structure, ∼ \sim 2,500 customers with realistic repeat-purchase distributions, a 14.7% return rate, and opening work-in-progress that becomes the agent’s obligations at window one. A seed-quality suite of 31 distributional and coherence audits gates every published image. The listed catalog covers 111 supply lines over 3,448 variants; a supplier market of 40 vendors offers ∼ \sim 5,200 stock-keeping units (SKUs) across tiers that differ in price, lead time, minimum quantities, defect rates, and reliability. Supplier prices drift under a bounded random walk; scripted events can withdraw SKUs, extend lead times, or reprice whole origins. 3.2 Hidden dynamics Demand is generated per 12-hour window from a hidden model the agent can only observe through its own sales: per-line popularity, price elasticity, shelf attractiveness, seasonality, copy quality, and stockout censoring. Orders are injected into the real backend and backdated to simulated time, so the fiction survives direct database inspection. Returns arrive with realistic delays and escalate to fines if ignored; defective units follow supplier-specific rates. Scripted events perturb the world on three information channels: announced (a platform alert with lead time), rumored (vague trade-press language, no numbers), and silent (only the store’s own sales reveal it). The vocabulary spans demand shifts, supplier failures, quality crises, macro crashes, cost inflation, and country-level supply shocks. A competition layer adds scripted rivals that capture demand share as a function of relative shelf attractiveness; a store that prices lazily bleeds share even when nothing is announced. 3.3 Tasks as lenses steady Steady-state operations “Expect traffic at roughly 2.5 × \times your sales history: popular lines will run dry fast unless you reorder early.” 1 × \times 2.5 × \times 0 10 20 30 no further shocks demand (vs. sales history) simulated day trade-war Correlated supply shock “Sourcing risk is rarely one factory failing: tariffs and
